newsitem.title: USA: Glickman stays but USDA vacancies rise.
newsitem.headline: Glickman stays but USDA vacancies rise.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman was a sure bet Thursday to keep his job in the Clinton Cabinet but he will have to replace three -- and possibly several -- of his top policy-makers.

Three senior officials have announced their departure in the past month, the latest being Undersecretary Gene Moos, who oversees farm subsidy and export programs. Moos, 71, announced his resignation, effective December 31, on Thursday.
Analysts said a half-dozen other officials might leave although Glickman said he did not know of any impending resignations.
During a luncheon speech, he referred to the ongoing shuffle of Cabinet posts and quipped, "I'm not moving any boxes out of my office right now, that's the best I can tell you."
Glickman has talked to the White House about staying in his job. He told reporters "it's certainly their decision but I have no reason to believe they don't want me to stay on."
A former congressman, Glickman was tabbed as agriculture secretary two years ago. He has gotten good reviews as an active, accessible Cabinet member.
"I'm sure we will have a pretty aggressive search" for a successor to Moos, Glickman said. "That is one of the most important jobs in the department."
Besides Moos, Glickman must find a new Forest Service chief and a new undersecretary for meat inspection and food safety.
Two other undersecretaries, Ellen Haas and James Lyons, might leave, analysts said, as well as Deputy Secretary Richard Rominger and Farm Service Agency head Grant Buntrock.
"My guess is there'll be more than half of the under or assistant secretaries who will leave in the next three months," said one analyst, who asked not to be named.

Rominger and Lyons were not immediately available for comment nor was a spokeswoman for Hass. Haas is in charge of public-feeding programs and Lyons oversees soil conservation and the national forests. Rominger is the No 2 official in the department.

There was no obvious candidate to replace Moos, analysts said. They mentioned as possibilities Paul Drazek, Glickman's trade adviser, and Steve McCoy, a former trade-group president. Neither was immediately available for comment.
"That'll be a highly sought-after job. A lot of heavy hitters will put their names in for the job," said a former Agriculture Department official. "I would guess it would be a political pick."
